newsitem.title: USA: Budget agreement put in writing.
newsitem.headline: Budget agreement put in writing.

text.p: The White House and congressional leaders put in writing a budget agreement Thursday to wipe out the deficit in five years, give $85 billion in net tax cuts and $209 billion in net savings.
The tax cuts would include a broad-based permanent capital gains reduction, "significant" inheritance tax relief, a $500 per child tax credit and expansion of Individual Retirement Accounts.
The agreement on taxes was spelled out in a letter to President Clinton from House Speaker Newt Gingrich, a Georgia Republican, and Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott, a Mississippi Republican.
Clinton got a commitment for "roughly" $35 billion over five years for education tax credits and deductions.

The House and Senate leaders also promised to try and include proposals such as a welfare-to-work tax credit, capital gains tax relief for home sales and proposals to clean-up urban toxic waste sites.

"There is a verbal agreement they will not turn to low income housing tax credit, EITC (earned income tax credit), or pension reversion as sources of funds," White House Legislative Director John Hilley said.
A letter from Gingrich and Lott to White House Chief of Staff Erskine Bowles stated that the tax proposals would not "cause costs to explode in the outyears."
There had been some concern among the Democrats that the tax cuts would balloon after the initial five years and could cause deep deficit in the first decade of the next century.
"This is exactly what we agreed to on that Friday, May 2, and I have to compliment Senator Lott and the Speaker that they were absolutely true to their word on every item," Hilley said.

On the spending side, the budget deal would have five-year savings of $77 billion in defence and $64 billion in domestic programmes below costs if current policies were continued unchanged through 2002.
Savings on the Medicare health programme for the elderly would be $115 billion over five years, and for the Medicaid programme for the poor there would be $13.6 billion in savings.
Spending for new programmes sought by Clinton would increase $32 billion through 2002.

The agreement would increase the budget deficit to $90 billion in fiscal 1998 from an expected $67 billion in 1997, according to a Senate Budget Committee summary. The deficit would then head lower until 2002 when there would be a federal surplus of $1 billion.
There would be a surplus in each of the next five years, ending $18 billion in the black in 2007.
The budget agreement used Congressional Budget Office economic assumptions of 2.1 percent annual economic growth.
White House negotiators said they believed the economy would perform better than that, but had been forced to accept the more conservative economic estimates.
A stronger economy makes reducing the deficit easier because it increases revenues taken in by the Treasury.
There were no assurances for funding for national service programmes such as AmeriCorps or Goals 2000 educational programmes, Hilley said.

Vice President Al Gore's energy conservation programme was not protected from cuts, but the administration did get assurances that Superfund and the Environmental Protection Agency would be spared cuts, Hilley said.
The negotiators agreed to implement the budget through two pieces of legislation, allowing for separate votes on spending and taxes.
"It was an absolute drop dead issue for the president to have two bills," Hilley said.

The spending bill would be considered first, followed by the tax bill, he said. "I think there will be an overwhelming vote of both parties for the budget bill and then members will choose their own path on the tax bill," Hilley said.
